idiom_name: lazy val gate + Either/Option at the use, cats Validated for accumulating errors
implementation_notes: Scala has the deferral primitive in the language: a lazy val evaluates its right-hand side the first time the value is accessed and caches the result (Scala 2.13 specification, value definitions), so a check computed in a lazy val runs once, on first use, and the outcome travels in Either or Option instead of an exception. The gate is a use-named method that folds over that value; when the caller must see every violation at once, cats' Validated (ValidatedNel) replaces Either's short-circuit with accumulating composition. Hand-rolled validator classes remain justified when rules are loaded at runtime or shared across types, but for ordinary domain types the lazy val plus Either is the whole structure.
pitfalls: lazy val is not free: the first access synchronises and every read afterwards passes a volatile or bitmap check, which is measurable in a hot path or per element of a large collection.
If the initializer throws, the value is not considered initialised, so a later access runs the initializer again - a transient failure is retried silently and an expensive check can repeat.
A lazy val is a hidden field plus a flag, so serialisation and reflection see uninitialised state; recompute the check after deserialisation instead of trusting a carried-over flag.
